archetype.name: Pocket Passer (timing-and-rhythm)
archetype.definition: A 38-year-old rhythm thrower who wins from a clean pocket on schedule, living off short completions to his tight ends and play-action shots, and gives nothing as a runner.

report.headline: Vintage Cousins underneath, but red-zone TD pace and middle-field misses won't hold
report.take:
Cousins looks like the Minnesota-era version of himself again, not the 2025 Falcons version. Last year he ranked 46th in CPOE at -2.8 and averaged 6.4 yards per attempt. This year he is back to +2.28 CPOE, 7.13 YPA and 0.169 EPA per dropback, 15th of 42. His intended air yards are up to 8.76 from a 6.9 aDOT last season. That fits a Kubiak offense that puts him under center on 43 of his plays and asks him to hit timing throws rather than dink. The profile is familiar: average aggressiveness (13.9%), a 2.98-second time to throw, and a 23.8% pressure-to-sack rate in line with the 20-28% band he has sat in for years. A deliberate pocket passer is going to take some sacks when the picture isn't clean, and that is the cost of the style, not a new flaw.

The season rests on two things. The first is the short game. Throws of 0-9 air yards produced +0.306 EPA on 78 attempts with 6 TDs and no picks. The second is a cleaner pocket than usual: he was pressured on only 14.1% of dropbacks, second-lowest of 32. Brock Bowers is the engine at +0.568 EPA per target. Tre Tucker (+0.354) and Michael Mayer (+0.264) carry real weight too. A defense ranked 2nd in EPA keeps games close, and 131 of his 152 dropbacks came within one score, where he has been good (+0.223).

The 11 touchdowns, first in the league, overstate him. Nine came on 26 red-zone attempts, and his red-zone success rate is only 37%. Those are touchdowns cashed rather than drives dominated, and his 7.6% TD rate is far above anything his long career suggests he sustains. The deep line (+0.776 EPA on 17 attempts) is too small a sample to lean on. The real weakness sits in between. On 10-19 yard throws he is completing 45% at -10.7 CPOE, and all four of his interceptions came there. Throws over the middle run -12.2 CPOE. Those are the throws an aging arm has to drive into tight windows, and they are where his turnovers come from.

The trend is up, with passing EPA rising each week from 0.4 to 9.8. Week 4 against Kansas City also showed the limits. Without guard Jackson Powers-Johnson he held the ball 3.28 seconds, the longest of his four starts, and posted -3 CPOE on 52 attempts. He piled up 365 yards on volume rather than precision. The run game ranks 29th in EPA, so when the offense has to throw it 50 times, it is Cousins carrying a load he handles adequately, not well.

strengths.title: Efficient short-area timing game
strengths.body: Cousins completes 74% of throws under 10 air yards at +3.9 CPOE. He has produced six touchdowns and no interceptions there. This is his career-long identity: an accurate, on-schedule thrower working with a scheme that gets tight ends open early. It should hold all year because it depends on skill and design, not luck.

strengths.title: Bowers-centered target tree
strengths.body: Bowers returns +0.568 EPA per target, and Tucker adds +0.354 as a secondary option, which gives Cousins two high-value reads. The tree is tight-end heavy, with Bowers and Mayer at 24 targets each. That suits a quarterback who wants to throw to space over the middle short rather than fit balls into tight windows downfield.

strengths.title: Rebound to his prime-level accuracy
strengths.body: His CPOE has flipped from -2.8 in 2025 to +2.28, and his YPA is back above 7. That matches his 2021-2022 Minnesota seasons, so it looks like the scheme fit restoring his norm rather than a fluke. A clean pocket so far (2nd-lowest pressure rate) helps, and that is the part most at risk.

concerns.title: Intermediate middle is the turnover zone
concerns.body: All four of his interceptions came on 10-19 yard throws, where he completes 45% at -10.7 CPOE. Middle-of-field throws sit at -12.2 CPOE. This is a real limitation for a 38-year-old: those throws need velocity into closing windows. Expect the interception risk to stay concentrated there.

concerns.title: Red-zone TD rate due to fall
concerns.body: Nine touchdowns on 26 red-zone attempts sits alongside a 37% red-zone success rate, which means few failed series turned into scores far more often than usual. His 7.6% TD rate (8th) is well above what his career production supports. Touchdown output should drift toward two or fewer a game.

concerns.title: Volume tied to a broken run game
concerns.body: The offense ranks 29th in rush EPA. When the Raiders fall behind, Cousins absorbs heavy volume, as in the 52 attempts against KC with a 3.28-second time to throw and negative CPOE. Jeanty's 25 targets return -0.062 EPA each, so the checkdown valve isn't productive. That is mostly role, not Cousins, but it caps his efficiency in high-volume games.

trend.note: Game passing EPA climbed every week (0.4, 6, 9, 9.8). Week 1's 17% bad-throw rate looks like rust. Week 4's big yardage came on volume and negative CPOE, so the climb is in production more than precision.

nextGame.headline: Stingy pass defense missing its top corner, soft against deep shots
nextGame.body:
New England's pass defense ranks 5th in EPA and allows QBs only 218 yards a game (5th-fewest), so on paper this is a firm test for a pocket passer. The cracks are specific. The Patriots rank 22nd against deep passes and 31st against the run. Their pass rush is middling (19th in sack rate, 17th in hit rate), which should let Cousins keep working from the clean pocket his game depends on.

Availability tilts toward Las Vegas. Christian Gonzalez, a 95%-snap corner, is out, and Charles Woods is questionable. That thins a secondary Cousins can test outside, where his numbers are strongest. Christian Barmore is also out, weakening an already soft run front. On the Raiders side, Powers-Johnson (groin) carries a return date of this game after missing Week 4, and his status matters for Cousins' pocket. Nailor (concussion) is questionable and Dont'e Thornton may return from IR. Neither changes the Bowers-first target tree.

keyMatchups.title: Jeanty against 31st-ranked run defense
keyMatchups.body: New England allows +0.028 EPA per rush, 31st in the league, the one matchup where Las Vegas' broken run game could function. If it does, Cousins gets lower volume, but also play-action looks and shorter third downs. That is the script where he is most efficient.

keyMatchups.title: Shots outside without Gonzalez
keyMatchups.body: The Patriots allow +0.683 EPA on deep throws (22nd), and their best corner is out. Cousins' deep sample is only 17 attempts, but they have produced three scores and he throws better to the sidelines than the middle. A couple of outside shots to Tucker are the likeliest big plays.

keyMatchups.title: Raiders defense shortening the game
keyMatchups.body: Las Vegas' defense is 2nd in EPA and 2nd in hit rate, facing a Patriots offense 20th in pass EPA. A close, low-possession game keeps Cousins in neutral situations where he has been sharp. It also limits his ceiling for yards.

nextGame.watch: Whether Powers-Johnson plays, and whether Cousins' time to throw drifts back toward the 3.28 seconds of Week 4 or stays under 3 seconds.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is sustainable: short-area accuracy, a productive tight-end core, and an elite defense keeping games close. Expect efficiency in the 0.10-0.17 EPA-per-dropback range, roughly where his better Minnesota seasons lived. The touchdown pace will not last. Nine red-zone scores on a 37% red-zone success rate and a 7.6% TD rate point to something nearer 1.5-2 touchdowns a week. The intermediate-middle interceptions are likely to keep coming at about one a game.

Volume is the swing. With a 29th-ranked run game, Las Vegas will lean on him whenever it trails, which can mean yardage spikes like Week 4. A defense this good also means plenty of games where 30 attempts is enough. Health of the interior line matters most at his age and with his style. His pressure rate has been unusually low, and any move toward league-average pressure will hurt a 2.98-second time to throw.

bets.reason: Las Vegas is 4-0 against the spread, and its 2nd-ranked defense faces a New England offense 21st in EPA. The Patriots are also missing their top corner and a starting DT. A field-goal-plus spread in a game likely decided by one score favors the dog.
The obvious read is to ride his league-leading 11 touchdowns. But nine came in the red zone on a 37% success rate, and New England allows only 1.5 QB TDs a game. Expect regression toward one or two.

He has thrown a pick in three of four games. All four came on intermediate throws, where he completes 45%. New England's 5th-ranked pass defense is strongest against the short and middle game, which pushes him toward those throws.

confidence.note: Four games and small depth splits, but the profile matches his long career.
